scenes.narration: It began around 114 BCE when the Han dynasty sent Zhang Qian into Central Asia.
Traders moved porcelain and textiles across land and maritime routes.
The roads spread religions like Buddhism and Islam into China.
Paper documents served as passports for travelers crossing nomadic lands.

facts.text: The Silk Road was a network of Asian trade routes active from the second century BCE until the mid-15th century.
facts.quote: The Silk Road was a network of Asian trade routes active from the second century BCE until the mid-15th century.

facts.text: The main route of the western regions of the Maritime Silk Road directly crosses the Indian Ocean from the northern tip of Sumatra to Sri Lanka, southern India and Bangladesh, and the Maldives.
facts.quote: The main route of the western regions of the Maritime Silk Road directly crosses the Indian Ocean from the northern tip of Sumatra (or through the Sunda Strait) to Sri Lanka, southern India and Bangladesh, and the Maldives.

facts.text: The Silk Road spanned over 6,400 km (4,000 mi) on land.
facts.quote: Spanning over 6,400 km (4,000 mi) on land,

facts.text: Secondary routes passed through the coastlines of the Bay of Bengal, the Arabian Sea, and southwards along the coast of East Africa to Zanzibar, the Comoros, Madagascar, and the Seychelles.
facts.quote: Secondary routes also pass through the coastlines of the Bay of Bengal, the Arabian Sea, and southwards along the coast of East Africa to Zanzibar, the Comoros, Madagascar, and the Seychelles.

facts.text: Silk was used as a tax payment and salary by Chinese farmers and civil servants under the Han dynasty.
facts.quote: Chinese farmers paid their taxes in silk. Civil servants received their salary in silk.

facts.text: In 198 B.C.E., the Han dynasty made a treaty with the Xiongnu, agreeing to give the Xiongnu ruler the emperor's daughter and pay annual gifts of gold and silk.
facts.quote: In 198 B.C.E., the Han dynasty concluded a treaty with a Central Asian people, the Xiongnu. The emperor agreed to give his daughter to the Xiongnu ruler and pay an annual gift in gold and silk.

facts.text: By the 1st century B.C.E., silk reached Rome, initiating the first "Silk Road."
facts.quote: By the 1st century B.C.E. silk reached Rome, initiating the first "Silk Road."

facts.text: Pliny thought silk was made from the down of trees in Seres and considered it very popular among Romans.
facts.quote: Pliny, writing about silk, thought it was made from the down of trees in Seres.

facts.text: Silk was associated with wealth and power, such as Julius Caesar entering Rome in triumph under silk canopies.
facts.quote: Julius Caesar entered Rome in triumph under silk canopies.

facts.text: Historians identify three main periods of Silk Road trade, including the Han to Rome period (206 B.C.E. to 220 C.E.) and a period during Tang dynasty China coinciding with the expansion of major religions into Central Asia (618 to 907 C.E.).
facts.quote: Conventionally, historians refer to three periods of intense Silk Road trade: 1) from 206 B.C.E. to 220 C.E., between the ancient Chinese Han dynasty and Central Asia, extending to Rome; 2) from about 618 to 907 C.E., between Tang dynasty China and Central Asia, Byzantium, the Arab Umayyad and Abbasid empires, the Sasanian Persian Empire, and India, and coinciding with the expansion of Islam, Buddhism, Assyrian Christianity, Zoroastrianism, Manicheism, and Judaism into Central Asia.

facts.text: The Silk Road term was coined by Baron Ferdinand von Richthofen in the 19th century
facts.quote: The term Silk Road (die Seidenstrasse) was first coined by the nineteenth-century German explorer Baron Ferdinand von Richthofen (1833-1905).

facts.text: Silk Road routes stretched from China to across the Eurasian continent to Europe
facts.quote: It broadly describes the ancient trading routes stretching across the Eurasian continent from China to Europe.

facts.text: Silk was one of the earliest and most important commodities traded on the Silk Road
facts.quote: While silk was clearly one of the earliest and most important commodities traded along the route,

facts.text: Precious metals, stones, spices, porcelain, and textiles were also traded along the Silk Road
facts.quote: precious metals and stones, spices, porcelain, and textiles also traveled the road.

facts.text: Silk Road enabled the spread of technologies like silk production, paper making, gunpowder, and block printing to the west
facts.quote: The technologies of silk production, paper making, gunpowder manufacture, and block printing made their way west across Asia via this highway.

facts.text: Religions including Buddhism, Islam, and Christianity spread to China via the Silk Road
facts.quote: Buddhism, Islam, and Christianity entered China via the Silk Road.

facts.text: The book was published in 2010 as part of the University of Pennsylvania Press Encounters with Asia series.
facts.quote: Buddhism and Islam on the Silk Road is a 2010 book by Johan Elverskog, published by the University of Pennsylvania Press as part of the Encounters with Asia series.

facts.text: The book covers Buddhist–Muslim relations across Inner Asia from Afghanistan to Mongolia from the eighth century through the nineteenth century.
facts.quote: Elverskog investigates the history of Buddhist–Muslim relations across Inner Asia, from Afghanistan to Mongolia, over a period spanning from the eighth century through the nineteenth century.

facts.text: The Mongol conquests of the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries brought Buddhists and Muslims together under a single political regime.
facts.quote: The Mongol conquests of the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries shattered the earlier division of Eurasia into separate economic zones, bringing Buddhists and Muslims together under a single political regime.

facts.text: Mongol rulers such as Hülegü and Khubilai Khan supported both Buddhist and Muslim traditions simultaneously.
facts.quote: Rulers such as Hülegü and Khubilai Khan supported both traditions at once, and the presence of Tibetan lamas, Uygur Buddhists, and Muslim scholars at Mongol courts created conditions for new forms of exchange.

facts.text: Rashid al-Din, the Il-khanid vizier, wrote a detailed and sympathetic Muslim account of Buddhism that portrayed the Buddha as a prophet.
facts.quote: Elverskog gives particular attention to Rashid al-Din, the Il-khanid vizier whose Compendium of Chronicles he regards as the most detailed and sympathetic Muslim account of Buddhism written before the modern era, one that presented the Buddha as a prophet and drew parallels between Buddhist and Islamic concepts.

facts.text: The Silk Road closure marked the end of over-land trade between East and West
facts.quote: The closure of the Silk Road initiated the Age of Discovery (also known as the Age of Exploration, 1453-1660 CE) which would be defined by European explorers taking to the sea and charting new water routes to replace over-land trade.

facts.text: The Age of Discovery began in 1453 CE following the Silk Road closure
facts.quote: The closure of the Silk Road initiated the Age of Discovery (also known as the Age of Exploration, 1453-1660 CE) which would be defined by European explorers taking to the sea and charting new water routes to replace over-land trade.

facts.text: European explorers sought new sea routes to access Asian goods after the Silk Road closed
facts.quote: The closure of the Silk Road initiated the Age of Discovery (also known as the Age of Exploration, 1453-1660 CE) which would be defined by European explorers taking to the sea and charting new water routes to replace over-land trade.

facts.text: The Silk Road operated from opening until closure, spanning many centuries
facts.quote: The Silk Road - from its opening to its closure - had so great an impact on the development of world civilization that it is difficult to imagine the modern world without it.

facts.text: Silk Road enabled cultural exchange and broadened world understanding among civilizations
facts.quote: In its time, the Silk Road served to broaden people's understanding of the world they lived in; its closure would propel Europeans across the ocean to explore, and eventually conquer, the so-called New World of the Americas initiating the so-called Columbian Exchange by which goods and values were passed between those of the Old World and those of the New, universally to the detriment of the indigengous people of the New World.

facts.text: Silk Road closure led to European exploration and colonization of the Americas
facts.quote: its closure would propel Europeans across the ocean to explore, and eventually conquer, the so-called New World of the Americas initiating the so-called Columbian Exchange by which goods and values were passed between those of the Old World and those of the New, universally to the detriment of the indigengous people of the New World.

facts.text: Silk Road travelers used paper documents as passports to cross nomadic lands or stay at caravansaries.
facts.quote: On the Silk Road, travelers carried paper documents that served as passports to cross nomadic lands or spend the night at a caravansary, a Silk Road oasis.

facts.text: Paper was the most important medium for spreading new systems of thought, especially religion, along the Silk Road.
facts.quote: But the most important function of paper along the Silk Road was that it was bound into texts and books that transmitted entirely new systems of thought, especially religion.

facts.text: Buddhism spread to China around the same time that paper became prevalent in the region.
facts.quote: It’s not a coincidence that Buddhism spread to China around the same time that paper became prevalent in the region,” says Wen.

facts.text: Manichaeism and Zoroastrianism also spread to China via the Silk Road alongside paper.
facts.quote: Same with Manichaeism and Zoroastrianism. One of the central significances of the Silk Road is that it served as a channel for the spread of different ideas and cultural interactions, and much of that relied on paper.

facts.text: Spices like cinnamon from Sri Lanka and cassia from China were exotic and coveted trade items on the Silk Road.
facts.quote: Spices from East and South Asia, like cinnamon from Sri Lanka and cassia from China, were exotic and coveted trade items, but they didn’t typically travel the overland routes of the Silk Road.

facts.text: Spices were mainly transported along an ancient maritime Silk Road linking port cities from Indonesia westward through India and the Arabian Peninsula.
facts.quote: Instead, spices were mainly transported along an ancient maritime Silk Road that linked port cities from Indonesia westward through India and the Arabian Peninsula.
